title: One unflagged week, week 51, decides the year
detail: The pre-Christmas week is the largest week of every year: $80.9M chain-wide on 2010-12-24, 75% above the median week. Thanksgiving week 47 is second at +40%. Between them these two weeks decide Q4, and the chain swings from a $40M trough to an $81M peak inside one year.
action: Plan labour, inventory and promotion against weeks 47-52 specifically, not a generic Q4.

title: The IsHoliday flag points at the wrong weeks
metric: 3 of the 5 biggest weeks are flagged as normal
detail: The Christmas flag falls on the week ending 31 Dec, which is the dead week after Christmas Day: those weeks average $43.2M against a December baseline of $61.3M, a -29% shortfall. Meanwhile week 51 carries no flag at all. Thanksgiving is the one flag that works, at +42%; Super Bowl and Labor Day sit inside normal weekly noise.
action: Replace the binary flag with named holiday features and a week-of-year index before forecasting.

title: Small-format stores are the most productive floor space
metric: Type C earns $1,667/sq ft vs $1,111 for Type A
detail: Type A stores are 4.4x larger and take 64% of revenue, but Type C extracts 50% more revenue from every square foot ($1,667 vs $1,111; Type B sits between at $1,163). The ranking by size and the ranking by productivity run in opposite directions, and ANOVA across formats is decisive (F=7,764, p<0.001).
action: Judge each format on revenue per square foot, and test small-format expansion rather than assuming bigger is better.

title: Macro conditions barely move the weekly till
metric: Temperature, fuel, CPI and unemployment explain 0.17% of variance
detail: A regression on the four economic indicators alone reaches R2=0.0017 - effectively nothing. Adding store size and the holiday flag lifts it to 6.1%, and aggregating to store-week reaches 67.2%, almost all of it from floor space. Structure beats sentiment: what a store sells is set by what it is, not by the economy that week.
action: Forecast from store, department and calendar; carry macro series only as a slow-moving overlay.

title: Markdown depth looks powerful until you control for store size
metric: $0.02 of sales per $1 of markdown, within store-dept
detail: Across records, the deepest markdown quintile averages $19,903 against $9,477 in the lightest, a 110% gap that looks like a strong promotion effect. It is mostly confounding: large departments receive large markdowns and already sell more. Removing each store-dept's own average leaves a slope of $0.015 per markdown dollar, explaining 0.1% of a store's own week-to-week swing. $2.82B of recorded markdown maps to roughly $42M of measurable movement, and the top quintile spends 2.4x the fourth for only 4pp more sales.
action: Stop reading the raw markdown-vs-sales curve as ROI; rebuild measurement with a holdout group before committing more spend.

title: Revenue is concentrated in a handful of departments
detail: Department 92 alone carries 7.2% of revenue ($484M), and the top ten take 46%. The bottom half of all departments contribute 8.7% between them.
action: Protect assortment and space in the top decile; review the long tail for delisting or consolidation.

title: Closing the productivity gap is the largest single prize
detail: 33 of 45 stores earn less per square foot than the top-quartile benchmark of $1,390. Lifting every one of them to that benchmark would add 25% of revenue across the 143-week window with no new floor space. This is a ceiling rather than a plan: it assumes the benchmark is reachable everywhere, which location and catchment will limit.
action: Run a per-store productivity programme benchmarked on revenue per square foot, starting with the largest absolute gaps.

title: Sales are far from normal, which breaks naive models
detail: Weekly sales are strongly right-skewed with heavy tails. The Normal fit is rejected (KS=0.240, p<0.001) while log-normal fits far better (KS=0.097); a log transform pulls skew from 3.3 to -1.18. 8.4% of records fall outside the Tukey fences, yet they carry 40% of all revenue.
action: Model log sales or quantile targets, and never trim the high outliers - they are the business.

title: The chain is predictable week to week, and barely growing
detail: A trend-times-seasonality model refitted on the first 130 weeks predicts the held-out 13 weeks to within 1.81%, against 2.04% for a seasonal-naive benchmark. The underlying trend is close to flat at $18k per week on a $47M weekly base, so nearly all movement is calendar, not growth.
action: Treat the weekly number as highly forecastable and spend planning debate on the seasonal peaks and the store-mix question.
